newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Rugby league-Super League plans recruitment drive.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Rugby league-Super League plans recruitment drive.

text.p: Media baron Rupert Murdoch's Super League said on Tuesday it planned to recruit top players from clubs loyal to Australia's established rugby league body.
Super League chief executive John Ribot said his organisation wished to open negotiations with players under contract to the Australian Rugby League (ARL).
The move follows Super League's comprehensive legal victory over the ARL on Friday when an appeals court reversed an earlier ban and freed Murdoch's rebel competition to kick off next year.
"Super League believes that all players should have the freedom to chose which competition they wish to compete in," Ribot said in a statement.
Ribot said Super League lawyers believe the players will be able to switch camps because their current ARL contracts are invalid as they amount to an "unreasonable restraint of trade".

"The operation of the (ARL player contracts) is extremely confusing and uncertain but they appear to be designed to prevent the players choosing who they player for up to 10 years after their current (contract) expires without the support of any guaranteed employment," Ribot said.

Super League, backed by Murdoch's News Ltd media group, has recovered the initiative after being forced to scrap its planned launch in March because of an earlier court order barring it from starting in Australia before the year 2000.
The Federal Court originally ruled that all existing clubs, including eight teams loyal to Super League, had to honour agreements binding them to the ARL until then.
But rebel clubs were released from that commitment on Friday when the court upheld News Ltd's appeal and ruled that the loyalty pacts were invalid.
Reacting to Super League's statement, ARL spokesman John Brady said the loyalty agreements were in place and the onus was on Super League to prove they were invalid.
"The contracts will hold. They are in place and it simply doesn't make sense for us to have to go out and prove they are valid," he said.
The boards of two clubs loyal to the ARL, St George and Illawarra, were due to meet later on Tuesday to decide whether they should begin talks to join the Super League.
Friday's court ruling has raised the possibility of there being two rugby league competitions in Australia next year.

The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper reported on Tuesday that ARL chairman Ken Arthurson had offered to step aside to save the ARL and allow it to administer a single restructured competition in cooperation with Super League.
